name: Information bias
statement: People rate a diagnostic test as worth doing when no result it could return would change the treatment they would give.
meaning: Two unrelated concepts carry this name, and this entry is about the one from decision research. Baron, Beattie and Hershey set out a normative rule for when a question is worth asking. A question earns its keep only if some possible answer would lead to a different action. Their subjects rated tests as worth doing when no answer could change the treatment. Two patterns produced that result. In the first, the test reports on a possibility that would not be treated whatever it showed. In the second, the test moves the probability of a diagnosis that will be acted on either way. The other information bias belongs to epidemiology, where Althubaiti gives it as a synonym for misclassification and defines it as error arising from how study measurements are obtained. Recall bias sits inside that second concept as a form of self-reporting bias, and selection bias is its counterpart, covering error introduced when subjects enter the study rather than when data are collected. Nothing about the epidemiological term concerns what a decision maker chooses to find out. The mirror image of the decision-research sense, refusing to look at information that could change something, is filed here under the ostrich effect.

origin.who: Jonathan Baron, Jane Beattie and John C. Hershey
origin.where: Organizational Behavior and Human Decision Processes
origin.note: The second of two 1988 papers on diagnostic reasoning. Six experiments named three biases, congruence, information and certainty. Crossref's record carries only the main title and drops the subtitle that names them.

evidence: Experiment 4 asked subjects to rate medical tests for choosing between three diseases, A, B and C, with prior probabilities fixed at .64, .24 and .12. The instructions said that the most likely disease would be treated whether or not the test was done, and that a wrong choice would not be caught in time to switch. Ratings ran from 0, meaning worthless, to 100. Fourteen subjects were tested and twelve were analysed. Of ten cases, only two had a normative value above zero, and those two drew the highest mean ratings, 61 and 75. Six of the worthless cases drew mean ratings between 25 and 48. Cases 4 and 6 gave information about diseases that would not be treated whatever the result, and they were rated above the matched worthless Case 10, t(11) = 3.30, p < .005. Cases 5 and 7 could shift the probability of disease A, which would be treated in any case, and were rated above Cases 3 and 8, t(11) = 3.86, p < .005. Four subjects gave ten zero ratings between them across Cases 3 to 8, one writing that the patient has to be treated for disease A either way. The three earlier experiments show the same gap between what the model priced at nothing and what subjects paid attention to. In Experiment 1 the expected utility of the question was zero for a mean of 36 of the 60 questions, and the mean number of zero ratings was five. In Experiment 2 the figures were 24 of 45 and six. Thirty-three subjects were given two further worthless-test problems and asked to justify their answers aloud. A majority answered correctly, and the paper prints transcripts of subjects who defend a useless test, are asked what they would do with each result, and then abandon the defence. A separate effect from the same family is Bastardi and Shafir's. Their subjects were paid Princeton and Stanford undergraduate volunteers. They gave 140 of them a course to register for, taught by a professor the student had just learned was the less popular one, and 82 percent registered. Another 149 got the same choice with the professor unknown until the next day, and 56 percent waited to find out. Since more than four in five register under the worse outcome, the information was worthless for most of them. Of the 56 percent who waited, 27 percentage points then declined the course, so 29 percent of the uncertain group turned it down against 18 percent of the simple group, chi-square(1, N = 289) = 4.86, p < .03. In their admissions scenario, 261 students in the simple version and 278 in the uncertain version, rejection ran at 54 percent after pursuit against 43 percent without it, chi-square(1, N = 539) = 6.15, p < .02. Redelmeier, Shafir and Aujla surveyed 1,206 clinicians, 171 dialysis nurses, 461 practising urologists and 574 academic physicians, splitting each scenario into a version where the information was already in hand and a version where it had to be sought. Among the nurses, 65 percent were willing to donate a kidney after choosing to be tested and being found suitable, against 44 percent who knew they were suitable from the start, P = 0.007.

replication.headline: No repeat of the diagnostic-test experiment was found, so the size of the original effect rests on twelve subjects rating ten cases.
replication.detail: Searches were run over the 128 works Semantic Scholar recorded as citing the 1988 paper in August 2026, over PubMed, over Crossref and over the open web, looking for a study rerunning the tutone task or any close variant. None was found, with physicians or with anyone else. The closest thing in the field is older than the experiment rather than a repeat of it. Allman, Steinberg, Keruly and Dans interviewed 42 physicians who had ordered 62 liver-spleen scans to look for metastases, taking their pretest probabilities, their management plans for each likely result and the thresholds at which they would stop investigating. Thirteen of the 42, 31 percent, wanted certainty before ruling metastasis in, and half planned further tests even once their estimate had reached one of their own stopping thresholds. Baron and colleagues cite that paper, so it is an antecedent rather than a test of them. The nearest thing to a repeat is the pursuit effect of Bastardi and Shafir, which Redelmeier, Shafir and Aujla reproduced in 1,206 clinicians, and that is a different claim: it says that seeking information changes the weight later placed on it, not that a worthless test is rated as worth doing. Two incentivised studies show people paying for information that cannot alter an outcome. Bennett and colleagues had 80 participants pay real money for advance notice of a lottery result that their choice could not affect, and explain it by aversion to prolonged uncertainty. FitzGibbon, Komiya and Murayama ran five experiments with 150 adults and a preregistered experiment with 361 more, and found people paying to learn what they could have won. Neither uses a diagnostic test, and neither asks whether the answer would change an action.

limits: The original numbers come from small groups of paid volunteers recruited by a sign on a walkway at the University of Pennsylvania. Fourteen were tested for Experiment 4 and twelve analysed, nine of fourteen were analysed in Experiment 1, ten in Experiment 2 and twelve in Experiment 3. The measure is a rating on a 0 to 100 scale, not a decision to order anything, so a rating of 26 on a worthless test records interest rather than a test performed. Whether the tests are worthless at all depends on stipulations written into the instructions: no other test exists, the wrong treatment will not be discovered in time, and the most likely disease is treated regardless. Baron and colleagues negated the free-test assumption in interviews by asking whether the test was worth five dollars, and subjects said it was. They also report that many subjects performed the checks that others skipped, and write that the biases may be correctable. Nothing in the paper measures reassurance, prognosis or future decisions, which are ordinary reasons to test. On reassurance there is evidence, and it does not favour that defence. Rolfe and Burton pooled 14 randomised trials covering 3,828 patients tested for symptoms carrying a low pretest probability of serious disease. Three trials gave an odds ratio of 0.87 for illness worry, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.39. Two gave a standardised mean difference of 0.06 for non-specific anxiety, 95% CI -0.16 to 0.28, and ten gave 0.99 for long-term symptom persistence, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.15. Eleven trials measured later primary care visits with high heterogeneity, I2 = 80%, and dropping the outliers left an odds ratio of 0.77, 95% CI 0.62 to 0.96. Their conclusion is that such tests do little to reassure patients or resolve their symptoms, though they may cut further visits. That leaves prognosis and later decisions untested here. Jonathan Nelson's later argument that Bayesian diagnosticity is normatively flawed, read here from its abstract, targets a different norm from the one Baron's group used, which prices a question by whether it changes the action. No study was found that measures information bias in a clinician and then measures that clinician's test ordering.
misreadings: The commonest error is reaching for the wrong concept entirely. In epidemiology, information bias means misclassification, and Althubaiti treats self-reporting bias, measurement error bias and confirmation bias as its forms, with recall bias an example of the first. That family is about how a study records data. This entry is about what a decision maker chooses to find out, and the two share nothing but a phrase. This atlas carries the parts of the epidemiological family under their own names, recall bias and selection bias, and has no entry under the epidemiological reading of this one. The second error is citation drift between three papers Jonathan Baron published in 1988. Outcome bias appeared in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology with Hershey, priors and error costs appeared in the first diagnostic reasoning paper with Hershey, and information bias appeared in the second with Beattie and Hershey. The third error is treating Bastardi and Shafir as a replication. Their finding is that pursuing information makes people use it, so a course they would have taken anyway gets turned down once the disappointing news is sought rather than given. Baron's finding is that a test with no power to change the treatment is still called worth doing. The fourth error is reading over-testing statistics as measurements of this bias. Chen and colleagues found that 53 percent of 440,857 Medicare patients had at least one test in the month before cataract surgery, where routine preoperative testing is not recommended, and that the strongest predictor was which ophthalmologist managed the evaluation rather than anything about the patient. Stojan and colleagues found that 29 to 32 percent of fourth-year medical students wanted more testing even after being handed a post-test probability. Neither study measures a cognitive bias, and provider practice patterns, payment and liability are live alternatives. The last error is calling every demand for useless information irrational. Bennett and colleagues explain paid-for lottery previews by an aversion to waiting under uncertainty, which is a preference about experience rather than a failure to ask whether the answer changes anything.
